title: FFA Interpretation: The Resident's Masterclass
summary: Fluorescein Fundus Angiography (FFA) remains the gold standard for dynamic imaging of the retinal and choroidal circulation. This guide provides a deep-dive into the pathophysiology, phases, and diagnostic patterns required for fellowship-level interpretation.

sections.title: Fundamental Principles & Dye Dynamics
content: Sodium Fluorescein (C20H10Na2O5): Low molecular weight (376 Da), 80% protein-bound (albumin), 20% free (fluorescent).
Excitation Peak: 465–490 nm (Blue light filter).
Emission Peak: 520–530 nm (Yellow-green light filter).
Inner Blood-Retinal Barrier (BRB): Non-fenestrated retinal capillary endothelial cells (tight junctions).
Outer Blood-Retinal Barrier: Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE) zonula occludens.
Metabolism: Hepatic glucuronidation; Renal excretion (within 24-36 hours).

sections.title: The 5 Phases of the Normal Angiogram

rows: Cilioretinal arteries fill (if present). Patchy 'mottled' choroidal filling due to fenestrated choriocapillaris.
Rapid filling of retinal arteries. Flow is fastest in the center of the vessel.
Complete arterial filling; 'Laminar' flow in veins where dye lines the vessel walls but the center is dark.
Complete filling of veins. Maximum intensity of fluorescence.
Dye intensity fades; Disc staining occurs; Absence of dye in vessels.

branches: Pooling (Sub-retinal or Sub-RPE spaces - CSC, PED)
Leaking (Break in BRB - NVD/NVE, CME, Cystoid spaces)
Staining (Vessel walls, Sclera, Scars, Optic Disc)
Vascular Filling Defect (Capillary non-perfusion, Arterial occlusion, Venous occlusion)

sections.title: Window Defect vs. Leakage: The Critical Distinction
Pooling: Sub-RPE vs. Sub-Retinal
content: Sub-RPE Pooling: Seen in Pigment Epithelial Detachment (PED). Discrete, well-demarcated borders. Fills early and stays bright late.
Sub-Retinal Pooling: Seen in Central Serous Chorioretinopathy (CSC). Indistinct, fuzzy borders. Takes longer to fill than sub-RPE.
Classic CSC Pattern: 'Smokestack' appearance (10%) or 'Ink-blot' appearance (90%).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Anaphylaxis & Emergencies
content: Laryngeal Edema / Stridor: Immediate Epinephrine (0.3mg IM 1:1000).
Severe Hypotension / Shock: Fluid resuscitation and Trendelenburg position.
Bronchospasm: Use Beta-agonists or Aminophylline.
Extravasation of Dye: Can cause local necrosis/phlebitis. Use cold compresses.
Known severe allergy to fluorescein is an absolute contraindication.

sections.title: Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) Patterns
content: Early Phase: Subtle leakage from perifoveal capillaries.
Late Phase: Classic 'Petaloid' pattern due to dye accumulation in Henle's layer (Outer Plexiform Layer).
Irvine-Gass Syndrome: Post-cataract surgery CME; features disc leakage + petaloid macula.
Diabetes: Often more diffuse 'honeycomb' appearance.

content.explanation: C: Choroidal, A: Arterial, L: Laminar (AV), V: Venous, R: Recirculation, S: Staining (Late).

sections.title: Management of Adverse Reactions
content: Step 1: Immediate cessation of dye injection if patient complains of itching/shortness of breath.
Step 2: Monitor Vital Signs (BP, HR, SpO2).
Step 3: Mild (Nausea/Vomiting) - Reassurance, deep breathing, emesis basin.
Step 4: Moderate (Urticaria) - Oral or IV Antihistamines (Diphenhydramine 25-50mg).
Step 5: Severe (Anaphylaxis) - 0.3ml of 1:1000 Epinephrine IM; Call Code Blue/EMS; Oxygen 10L/min.

sections.title: Interpretation Algorithm: The 'Rule of 4'
content: 1. Analyze the Control Image: Look for autofluorescence and pseudofluorescence.
2. Verify the Quality: Check for media opacities (lens/vitreous) and timing.
3. Locate Abnormalities: Is it Hyper or Hypo? Use the Macula as the center reference.
4. Dynamic Evolution: Does the area change in size or intensity from 30s to 5min?

sections.title: Choroidal Neovascularization (CNV) Classification
content: Classic CNV: Well-defined, bright lacy pattern in early phase; intense late leakage that obscures boundaries.
Occult CNV (Type 1): Fibrovascular PED (irregular elevation) or 'Late Leakage of Undetermined Source'.
Retinal Angiomatous Proliferation (RAP - Type 3): Intraretinal hemorrhages and small anastomoses filling from retinal circulation.
Polypoidal Choroidal Vasculopathy (PCV): Best seen on ICG, but FFA shows 'stippled' hyperfluorescence and late pooling.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Fellowship Exams
content: Blocked fluorescence: Blood is the most common cause. Subretinal blood blocks choroidal AND retinal; Intraretinal blood blocks retinal vessels.
The Foveal Avascular Zone (FAZ): Normally 0.5mm; enlargement indicates ischemia (DR, RVO).
Staining vs. Leakage: Staining involves fixed borders (e.g., old scar); leakage involves expanding, fuzzy borders (e.g., active CNV).
Dark Choroid: A classic FFA sign of Stargardt Disease due to lipofuscin accumulation in RPE blocking choroidal flush.
